title: What Do We Mean When We Say "Times"?
author: Tom Manners
summary: Tom Manners interrogates a word maths teachers use constantly without examining it: 'times.' He describes a training-session exercise in which he asks attendees to draw a picture representing 'three times seven' and consistently gets two different, contradictory images back -- some drawing three groups of seven, others seven groups of three -- revealing genuine ambiguity in ordinary classroom language. Manners argues this isn't merely academic: understanding whether 'times' means 'lots of' in one order or the other shapes how children build a structural understanding of multiplication that later supports division (sharing vs. grouping) and scaling. He digs into how UK curriculum bodies actually define the convention -- NCETM's non-statutory guidance, its curriculum prioritisation materials, and major schemes including White Rose, CanDoMaths, and Maths No Problem -- and finds they broadly converge on treating 'number of groups x group size' as the standard structure, while explicitly avoiding 'multiplied by' and 'times by' phrasing because it implies the reverse order. The piece ends with a direct challenge to school leaders: is your staff actually consistent in how they use and explain 'times,' or has an unexamined ambiguity been left to confuse pupils?
points: Manners's key evidence is a live training demonstration: asking attendees to draw 'three times seven' reliably produces two contradictory pictures (3 groups of 7 vs. 7 groups of 3), showing the ambiguity is real and widespread among practitioners, not just theoretical.

He connects the ambiguity to later mathematical understanding -- being clear about 'number of groups x group size' matters for how children later interpret division (24 divided by 4 as sharing into 4 groups vs. finding how many groups of 4) and scaling.

His research into NCETM guidance finds explicit avoidance of 'multiplied by' and 'times by' phrasing specifically because those phrasings imply the multiplicand is stated first -- a subtle point most teachers have likely never been taught explicitly.

Cross-checking major UK schemes (White Rose, CanDoMaths, Maths No Problem) shows they converge on the same 'number of groups x group size' convention, giving Manners's argument practical backing beyond a single curriculum body.

The piece closes with an actionable challenge for school leaders rather than just an observation: is the convention actually applied consistently across a maths department, or left to individual teacher habit?
quotes: In training sessions, I regularly ask attendees to draw a picture to represent “three times seven.” Every single time, I get back two different images. Some people draw three lots of seven. Others draw seven lots of three.

If I said “seven three times,” it feels much clearer: I mean three lots of seven (the red counters above). So perhaps that’s the issue. Maybe the problem lies not in the word itself but when we say it?

Because the structure of the maths still matters. Understanding whether we mean "three lots of seven" or "seven lots of three" helps children develop a deeper understanding -- especially once we move into division.
It goes on to say that “multiplied by” and “times by” are not used as this implies the multiplicand (the group size) is written first followed by the multiplier (the number of groups).
But do your staff know this? Can you aim for an agreed decision to avoid confusion? Definitely something to keep in mind for all the times that you say "times".
